summary: Follow one page request from the moment you press Enter until the page appears.
goals: Learn how DNS finds a server and why its answers are cached.
See why opening a connection takes round trips.
Follow a request from browser to server to database and back.
See where page-load time is spent.
Compare a slow database query with a user far from the server.

steps.title: A page feels slow
body: To make a page faster, first find out where it spends time. Follow one request for a shopping page.
You type shop.example and press Enter. The page appears about 155 milliseconds later. Several computers have talked to each other along the way.
steps.callout: A web request is a conversation between computers. Each message takes time, so the delays add up.

steps.title: Find the server’s address (DNS)
body: People use names such as shop.example. Networks send data to an IP address, a number that identifies a computer on the network. The browser asks a DNS resolver to find the address for the name.
The resolver returns 203.0.113.7 in about 20 milliseconds.
steps.callout: A time to live (TTL) says how long the browser may reuse a DNS answer. While the answer is still valid, a repeat visit can skip this lookup.

steps.title: Open a secure connection
body: The browser connects to 203.0.113.7. A TCP handshake sets up the connection. A TLS handshake sets up encryption so other people on the network cannot read the traffic.
Each handshake needs a round trip: a message goes to the server and an answer comes back. Here one round trip takes 30 milliseconds, so the two handshakes take about 60 milliseconds.
steps.callout: Round-trip time (RTT) mostly depends on the network distance and route between the computers. A faster server cannot remove that travel time.

steps.title: Send the page request
body: The browser sends GET /products over the open connection. GET asks the server to return the product page.
The server reads the request, checks the user’s session, and runs the page code. This takes one more round trip plus about 10 milliseconds of server work.
changes: + Request: 1 round trip + 10 ms of server work

steps.title: The server reads the database
body: The product information is stored in a database, not in the web server. The server asks the database for the product rows, then waits for the answer.
Watch the request travel to the database and the data travel back.
steps.callout: A stateless server does not keep a user’s session only in its own memory between requests. Keeping shared data in a database lets any web server handle the next request, which helps when we add more servers.

steps.title: Send the page back
body: The server uses the database rows to build HTML and sends it to the browser. Downloading it takes about 20 milliseconds. The browser shows the page 155 milliseconds after you pressed Enter.
The browser then sees that the page needs images and style files. It sends more requests. Reusing the open connection means these requests do not need the handshakes again.

steps.title: Load the page’s other files
body: The HTML page also points to images, style sheets, scripts, and fonts—about 40 more files. The browser has to fetch those files too.

With HTTP/1.1, each connection usually handles one request at a time, so a browser opens several connections and queues the rest. HTTP/2 can carry many requests at once over one connection. This is called multiplexing.
steps.callout: Smaller files are quicker to send. Sites can bundle scripts, compress text, use modern image formats, and load below-the-fold content only when needed.

steps.title: Case: a slow database query
body: The shop adds a “recommended for you” box. For every page view, its database query sorts all products by a score. Now the database takes 400 milliseconds to answer.
The network and connection steps have not changed, but the page now takes more than half a second. Requests wait in line for the database.
steps.callout: Measure before changing code. In this case the network is fine; the slow query is the problem. The Indexes lesson shows one way to speed up some queries.

steps.title: Case: the user is far away
body: Return to the fast query, but open the page in Sydney while the server is in Virginia. Each round trip now takes about 200 milliseconds instead of 30.
The two connection handshakes plus the page request add about 600 milliseconds before the page downloads. The server and code are unchanged, but the page takes more than four times as long.
steps.callout: Reduce round trips by reusing connections and using newer network protocols. A content delivery network (CDN) stores copies of files on servers closer to users. Placing services in more regions can also reduce distance.

steps.title: Recap: where the time went
body: Of the 155 milliseconds, the server and database spend only about 25 milliseconds doing work. Roughly 130 milliseconds is time spent waiting for messages to cross the network.

• DNS finds an IP address for a name, and its answer can be cached.
  • Opening connections takes round trips; reuse connections when you can.
  • Server code may be a small part of the delay, unless a slow query holds things up.
  • Greater distance increases the time for every round trip.
steps.callout: Next: Latency & Throughput explains what happens to these delays when many users arrive at once.
